messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 39
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Construction Worker
  trauma_type: Witnessed other trauma
  pcl5: 73

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Suppress Anger: never allow myself to feel or express anger, Gambling: I gamble to distract myself or feel excitement, Dissociate Deliberately: deliberately try to leave my body or blank out
  Memory: Visual Memories: My memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images., Olfactory Recall: When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened., Taste Vividness: I can taste what I tasted during the event when the memory returns
  Negative Appraisals: Shattered Beliefs: My beliefs about how the world works have been completely destroyed, Helplessness: I can't stop bad things from happening to me, Inadequacy: I am inadequate

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Ethan, a 39‑year‑old construction worker, was still a teenager when the night the town’s historic rowhouse caught fire turned his world inside out. He had been on the crew that day, hammering nails into a porch that had been slated for renovation. The evening was unusually warm; the smell of fresh paint lingered in the air. Suddenly, a burst of orange light broke through the evening haze, and the fire's crackle cut through the quiet. Ethan’s eyes widened as the blaze consumed the wooden frame of the front kitchen, the flames licking the roof and the windows. The scream of his neighbor’s wife, her voice breaking, was a sound he would carry for years. The heat hit his face before the heat of the fire itself; he felt the hot air on his skin and smelled the acrid scent of burning wood that still lingered long after the fire trucks arrived. In the chaos he watched the neighbor’s son, a boy the same age as his younger brother, run into the house and emerge shivering, his face pale as ash. Ethan felt a sudden, unshakable sense of helplessness – that he could do nothing to stop the terror he witnessed. The memories of that night are not fleeting whispers; they come to him as vivid, isolated images. When he closes his eyes, the fire's orange blaze and the neighbor’s wife's frantic face overlay his own heartbeat. The scent of burning plaster and the taste of scorched bread that his wife had left on the counter the night before haunt him whenever he thinks about the scene. He swallows when the smell of smoke returns, the metallic taste of fear crawling to the back of his throat. This intense recall is compounded by the feeling that his senses were assaulted so strongly that the memories have become almost tangible. The memory’s clarity reinforces the belief that the world is a dangerous place where nothing can be stopped. He has come to believe that his worldview is broken. The experience shattered his fundamental assumptions about safety and competence. “The world is cruel and unforgiving,” he says, “and I can’t do anything to make it right.” The sense of helplessness, coupled with an acute sense of inadequacy, has hardened his belief that he cannot protect himself or those he loves. He insists that his anger is a threat; he suppresses it so tightly that he never allows himself to feel or express it. In the quiet hours of the night, he throws himself at a slot machine or bets on a horse race, hoping for the fleeting rush of excitement to drown the terror that gnaws at him. He deliberately tries to dissociate, to leave his body and stare at the ceiling as if it were a window to a calmer world, because he believes that feeling any emotion would bring him closer to the trauma he cannot escape. These maladaptive strategies feel like the only tools he has to keep the memories from seeping into his everyday life. When the sound of the construction site's hammering echoes across the open field, Ethan’s brain instantly flags the flashbacks. The memory surges, and the heat of that night returns, making him feel that the flames are about to ignite again. He finds himself pulling out of his shift before his supervisors notice, retreating to the truck to avoid the noise that triggers the vivid recollection. Over months, this avoidance has become routine; he misses half a day each week, missing crucial hours that he relies on for his livelihood. When he returns, his coworkers notice a tense edge, his focus broken. His partner has tried to reach out, but Ethan’s fear that his presence might attract danger keeps him distant, widening the chasm between them until their divorce became inevitable. The job has begun to feel more like a prison than a place of work, and his fear that the world is still dangerous drives him to stay away from the site, even when it is safer to be there. Ethan’s negative appraisals of the world have driven him toward these maladaptive strategies and the memories of the fire have reinforced his sense of helplessness and the belief that the world is broken. The memories, in turn, fuel his attempts to dissociate and suppress anger, further entrenching his distorted beliefs. In the first sessions, he reports relentless insomnia, waking up gasping, and a growing anxiety that the fire could return at any moment. The last month he has been unable to sleep on a normal mattress because the taste of charred wood lingers in his mouth, a constant reminder that his life remains forever tainted. The realization that he has lost a job, the end of his marriage, and the inability to share his pain with others have made him finally seek help. He fears that his anger and gambling will consume his family if nothing changes, yet he hopes that confronting the memories might free him from the endless cycle of avoidance and despair.
